previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: The patient, a woman with chronic pancreatitis, was admitted with a three-day history of epigastric abdominal pain radiating to the back, nausea, vomiting, and inability to tolerate oral intake. She was managed with NPO status, IV hydration, and IV pain and nausea medications, including dilaudid, toradol, promethazine, and Ativan. A midline catheter was placed on hospital day two for reliable IV access. Imaging showed constipation but no obstruction. Her symptoms improved over several days, allowing transition to oral medications and a regular diet. She was discharged home on her prior medication regimen with added stool softeners and laxatives. She is to follow up with her primary care provider and psychiatrist for ongoing management of pain and mental health.

radiology_notes.text:
INDICATION:  ___ year old woman with chronic pancreatitis and needs ___ for PICC
// has inpatient protocol. requires PICC

COMPARISON:  Comparison is made to picc line placement performed ___

TECHNIQUE:  OPERATORS: Dr. ___ radiology fellow) and Dr.
___ radiology attending) performed the procedure.  The
attending, Dr. ___ was present and supervising throughout the procedure.
ANESTHESIA: 1% lidocaine was injected in the skin and subcutaneous tissues
overlying the access site.
MEDICATIONS: Lidocaine.
CONTRAST: 0 ml of Optiray contrast.
FLUOROSCOPY TIME AND DOSE:  0.1 min, 2 mGy

PROCEDURE:
1. Single lumen PICC placement through the brachial vein on the right.

PROCEDURE DETAILS: Using sterile technique and local anesthesia, the brachial
vein on the right was punctured under direct ultrasound guidance using a
micropuncture set. Permanent ultrasound images were obtained before and after
intravenous access, which confirmed vein patency. A peel-away sheath was then
placed over a guidewire. The guidewire was then advanced into the superior
vena cava using fluoroscopic guidance. A double lumen PIC line measuring  cm
in length was then placed through the peel-away sheath with its tip positioned
in the distal SVC under fluoroscopic guidance. Position of the catheter was
confirmed by a fluoroscopic spot film of the chest. The peel-away sheath and
guidewire were then removed. The catheter was secured to the skin, flushed,
and a sterile dressing applied.
The patient tolerated the procedure well. There were no immediate
complications.

FINDINGS: 

1.  The accessed vein (a brachial vein) was patent and compressible.
2.  Brachialvein approach double lumen right PICC with tip in the distal SVC.

IMPRESSION: 

Successful placement of a right 38 cm brachial approach double lumen PICC with
tip in the distal SVC.  The line is ready to use.
